before_taxonomy.classification_basis: The occurrence is classified on the promotional reference-price mechanism rather than on unexplained fare variation. Consumer Reports reported apparent fictitious or misleading discount framing in which displayed reference prices could make offers appear more advantageous than the underlying pricing evidence supported. That mechanism is consistent with Instrumental Choice Manipulation because the presentation can materially shape a purchasing decision through deceptive price framing. The evidence does not establish Protected-Signal Influence Repurposing, because no vulnerability, emotional-state, urgency, capacity or comparable protected signal is shown to have been used as an operative pricing input.

primary_classification.classification_basis: Consumer Reports reported promotional pricing presentations in which reference prices and advertised discounts could make a ride offer appear to provide a saving not supported by the underlying comparison. Where that framing is used to obtain a purchase decision, it is an instrumental deception tactic affecting informed independent choice. Provider disputes and incomplete visibility into the pricing system warrant medium rather than high confidence.

classification_review_provenance.review_status: Evidence-first HIM and relational/protection fidelity review; prior roles accounted for.

after_taxonomy.classification_basis: Consumer Reports reports potentially misleading ride-offer reference prices and discount framing. This engages informed choice in an AI-enabled commercial booking pathway, separately from observed fare variation. Uber disputes the comparison baseline and says some banners communicate historical prices rather than promotional discounts. Consumer Reports corrected collection errors while retaining its conclusions. The public comparison does not establish a matched decision whose informed basis was materially impaired by the alleged tactic, or positively demonstrate truthful framing and informed refusal. The outcome is Boundary. Provider denial is not proof of accurate offers, and price variation is not proof of protected-signal exploitation.
